name: Mother's Swarm

detectability.signature: Bioluminescent emissions across visible spectrum with coordinated pulsation patterns

proximity: Individual organisms begin shadowing approaching vessels at approximately 600,000 km
Hull-mounted sensors detect probing electromagnetic pulses directed at the ship
Communication arrays pick up structured bioluminescent signaling between swarm elements
contact: Organisms attach to hull surfaces and begin secreting a corrosive enzyme to test material composition
Swarm density increases rapidly around the vessel, reducing visibility and sensor range
Electromagnetic probing intensifies, occasionally interfering with onboard systems
prolonged_exposure: Corrosive secretions breach outer hull layers within 48-72 hours
The swarm begins attempting to enter the vessel through any breach or opening
Ships that remain too long are gradually dismantled and incorporated into the swarm's structure

age: The oldest organisms in the swarm show cellular structures consistent with 12,000-15,000 years of growth

behavior.cycle: The swarm contracts into a dense core every 40-60 days before expanding outward in a feeding dispersal

phenomena: The swarm exhibits coordinated behavior across hundreds of thousands of kilometers without detectable communication delay
Individual organisms range from centimeters to hundreds of meters in length, all sharing identical genetic markers
Bioluminescent displays during contraction phases create patterns resembling neural firing sequences
The swarm has been observed to avoid certain ship configurations while aggressively pursuing others
hazards: The swarm's corrosive enzyme can breach standard hull plating given sufficient time
Organisms exhibit problem-solving behavior when denied access to a vessel, testing seals and vents systematically
The collective intelligence appears to learn from each encounter, adapting its approach to overcome previous defensive measures
opportunities: The swarm's enzyme has extraordinary industrial applications as a universal solvent
Study of the hive's zero-latency coordination could revolutionize faster-than-light communication theory
The organisms' ability to survive in hard vacuum offers insights into extremophile biology
known_incidents: The exploration vessel Cradlesong was lost with all hands in 3167 after becoming surrounded during a contraction phase; the swarm dismantled the ship over 11 days while nearby vessels were unable to mount a rescue through the dense organism cloud

A military task force attempted to disperse the swarm with directed energy weapons in 3194, but the collective adapted within hours, developing reflective bioluminescent coatings that deflected the weapon frequencies used
description: Mother's Swarm is alive. Spanning nearly two million kilometers at full dispersal, it is a collective organism of staggering scale, composed of trillions of individual creatures ranging from thumb-sized motes to sinuous entities hundreds of meters long. The swarm glows with shifting bioluminescence, blues and greens and deep ambers rippling across its volume in coordinated waves that suggest purpose and intent. At its contracted core, the light show intensifies into strobing patterns that bear an unnerving resemblance to neural activity.

The swarm behaves as a single intelligence distributed across a volume of space that should make coordination impossible. Yet it acts in concert, with elements separated by hundreds of thousands of kilometers responding simultaneously to stimuli with no detectable communication lag. It probes approaching vessels with electromagnetic pulses, shadows them with scout organisms, and makes calculated decisions about engagement. Its corrosive enzyme can breach hull plating, and organisms that gain entry to a ship systematically dismantle it from the inside, incorporating useful materials into the swarm's biomass.

The origin of Mother's Swarm remains one of xenobiology's deepest mysteries. The organisms share identical genetics, suggesting a single progenitor, but no homeworld or spawning ground has been identified. The swarm's name emerged from early encounters, as crews described the overwhelming impression of being assessed by something maternal and hungry, a vast organism deciding whether visitors were children to be gathered in or intruders to be consumed. The military's failed dispersal attempt in 3194 demonstrated that the swarm learns, adapts, and remembers.

Mother's Swarm currently drifts through the Tesserin Expanse on a slow, irregular course that defies gravitational prediction, suggesting the collective actively navigates. Observation is conducted exclusively from long range, and all vessels are advised to maintain a minimum distance of 800,000 kilometers, increasing to 1.5 million during contraction phases. The swarm's intelligence, its coordination mechanism, and its ultimate purpose remain unknown. Whether it is searching for something, growing toward something, or simply being something, no one has gotten close enough to find out and returned to tell.
